segments.text: A thunderstorm swallows a paraglider and drags her nearly ten kilometres up, higher than Everest. No engine. No oxygen. Then she blacks out.
More than half an hour later, she wakes up. Covered in ice. Still flying.
No chance. Nobody passes out up there and lands alive. Let's go look.
Her name is {Ewa|Eva} {Wisnierska|Vishnyairska}. Born in Poland, flying for Germany, thirty-five years old. Two years earlier she won the Paragliding World Cup.
February {2007|two thousand seven}. Manilla, Australia. The world championships start in ten days, and more than a hundred pilots are here for a warm-up.
Around noon she launches from Mount Borah. Sunshine, small clouds. The forecast says thunderstorms are possible. Later.
The wind is from the south, so the pilots fly north. About two hours in, two clouds ahead of her grow. Then they join.
She tries to fly around it. Too late. Pilots call it cloud suck: the storm breathes in, and she is in the way.
So she does what pilots do. A spiral dive: wing on its side, dropping as fast as it can. Once. Twice. Three times. She is still going up.
Good lift is three or four metres a second. Her instruments log about twenty. I brought an umbrella. It did not help.
She radios her team leader on the ground. It is raining, it is hailing, and she is still climbing.
Inside, it is dark. Hail hammers her. Lightning cracks in front of her, behind her, all around.
In about fifteen minutes the storm carries her to nearly ten thousand metres. Up here it is around forty below zero, and the air is too thin to stay awake.
She blacks out. For more than half an hour the glider flies itself, sinking and lifting, its pilot hanging in the harness.
Doctors said later that passing out may be what saved her. Unconscious, her body needed less oxygen.
Then she wakes up. Her gloves are frozen. The brake handles are cased in ice. She scratches the ice off her GPS. She is still almost seven thousand metres up.
But the wing is open and flying. She takes the brakes and spirals down. This time, it works.
About three and a half hours after take-off, she lands beside a farm, roughly sixty kilometres from where she started.
Her radio is dead. Then her phone rings. It is her team. She sends them her position, and they come and get her.
Frostbite on her ears and face. Bruises from the hail. About an hour in hospital, and she is out.
The event's organiser put her odds at winning the lottery ten times in a row.

The storm did not let everyone go. {He|Huh} {Zhongpin|Jong-pin}, forty-two, flew for China and had more than ten years in the air. The same cloud took him. He was found the next day. A post-mortem found he had been struck by lightning.

{Ewa|Eva} kept flying. She had her height, {9946|nine nine four six}, stitched onto her glider. In {2010|twenty ten} her flight became a documentary, Miracle in the Storm. Today she teaches paragliding in Bavaria.
Pulled up past Everest, out cold, and she landed it herself. I was wrong. Case closed.
